summary: Describes how to use the SHAKE hash function family with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. It updates RFC 3279 with algorithm identifiers and conventions for this use.

eli5.summary: Signatures need a mixing machine to boil a document down. This adds a newer mixing machine called SHAKE to the list certificates may use.

subtitle: Algorithm identifiers that let X.509 certificates and CRLs use the SHAKE hash functions with RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA signatures.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates and revocation lists had no identifiers for signatures built on the SHAKE functions of the SHA-3 family.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8692 defines four object identifiers, for RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA with each of SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. It fixes the SHAKE output lengths, salt length and mask generation, and requires absent parameters.
tldr.outcome: CAs and clients can encode and recognize SHAKE-based signatures and public keys. The RFC updates RFC 3279 and gives key size guidance for each SHAKE.

today: RFC 8692 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 3279. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: SHAKE Meets X.509
sections.content:
RFC 3279 defines algorithm identifiers for the X.509 certificate and CRL profile in RFC 5280. RFC 8692 updates it with identifiers for algorithms built on the variable-length SHAKE functions from the SHA-3 standard (FIPS 202).

The SHA-3 family has two extendable-output functions, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. A SHAKE is written SHAKE(M, d): it produces a digest of d bits for message M. The other four SHA-3 instances (SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, SHA3-512) are out of scope. A SHAKE can serve as the message digest in RSASSA-PSS (RFC 8017) and ECDSA, and as the hash inside the mask generation function (MGF) of RSASSA-PSS.
sections.eli5: SHAKE is a machine that boils any document down to a short fingerprint. The fingerprint can be as long as you ask. This RFC says how certificates can name it.

sections.title: The Four Identifiers
sections.content:
Four new object identifiers (OIDs) are defined under the PKIX algorithms arc: id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128 (30), id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256 (31), id-ecdsa-with-shake128 (32) and id-ecdsa-with-shake256 (33). The same RSASSA-PSS identifiers can also identify a public key.

For all four, the parameters MUST be absent, so the AlgorithmIdentifier is a SEQUENCE of one component: the OID. In summary, when hashing the message to be signed, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 output 256 and 512 bits respectively.
sections.eli5: Each recipe gets its own name tag. The tag alone says everything, so no extra notes are stapled to it.

sections.title: RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA Rules
sections.content:
For RSASSA-PSS, the message hash and the MGF hash MUST be the same SHAKE. The message hash output is 32 bytes for SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for SHAKE256. The SHAKE is used natively as the MGF, instead of the MGF1 algorithm of RFC 8017. The MGF output length is (8*emLen - 264) bits for SHAKE128 or (8*emLen - 520) bits for SHAKE256, where emLen is ceil((n-1)/8) and n is the RSA modulus size in bits. For a 2048-bit modulus that gives 1784 or 1528 bits. The saltLength MUST be 32 bytes for SHAKE128 or 64 bytes for SHAKE256, and the trailerField MUST be 1 (hexadecimal 0xBC). The hash, mask generation, trailer and salt are all embedded in the OID, which is why no parameters are used.

For ECDSA, the matching SHAKE is the hash, and its output length d MUST be 256 bits for SHAKE128 or 512 bits for SHAKE256. CAs SHOULD generate such signatures with a deterministic, nonrandom k as required by RFC 6979. The older ECDSA standards do not list SHAKE, but SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 with 32 and 64 octet outputs can be used in place of 256- and 512-bit hashes such as SHA256 and SHA512.
sections.eli5: The recipe fixes every measurement: how long the fingerprint is, how much random seasoning to add, and which tool mixes things. Nobody gets to pick their own amounts.

sections.title: Signatures and Public Keys in PKIX
sections.content:
The new identifiers may be used in the signatureAlgorithm field of a Certificate and the signature field of TBSCertificate. A conforming CA MUST name the algorithms explicitly with these OIDs when encoding RSASSA-PSS or ECDSA with SHAKE signatures in certificates and CRLs. Conforming clients MUST recognize the OIDs. The RSA modulus and ECDSA curve order SHOULD be chosen in line with the SHAKE output length.

For public keys, rsaEncryption continues to identify an RSA key when the owner does not want to restrict it to RSASSA-PSS with SHAKEs. An owner who does want that restriction SHOULD use the RSASSA-PSS SHAKE identifiers in the SubjectPublicKeyInfo algorithm field. For ECDSA with SHAKE public keys, a CA MUST specify the algorithm explicitly with the OIDs. In every case the parameters MUST be absent.
sections.eli5: A certificate must write the exact recipe name on its signature, and anyone checking it must know how to read that name.

sections.title: IANA and the ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
IANA assigned decimal 94, id-mod-pkix1-shakes-2019, in the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry for the ASN.1 module in Appendix A. It added the four algorithm OIDs (30 to 33) to the SMI Security for PKIX Algorithms registry. It also added shake128 (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.11) and shake256 (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.12) to the Hash Function Textual Names registry.

Appendix A is a new ASN.1 module that references RFC 5912. It defines the SHAKE digest algorithms, the RSASSA-PSS public key types and the four signature algorithms, all with absent parameters.
sections.eli5: The official registry book now lists each new recipe name and its number, so everybody spells them the same way.

sections.title: Strength and Key Sizes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3279 apply here as well. NIST special publications SP 800-78-4 and SP 800-107 are named as guides for choosing key sizes.

SHAKE128 with a 256-bit output offers 128 bits of collision and preimage resistance. The SHAKE128 OIDs are RECOMMENDED with a 2048-bit RSA modulus (112-bit security), a 3072-bit modulus (128-bit security) or curves with a 256-bit group order (128-bit security). SHAKE256 with a 512-bit output offers 256 bits. The SHAKE256 OIDs are RECOMMENDED with a 4096-bit RSA modulus or higher, or curves with a group order of at least 512 bits, such as NIST Curve P-521. The RFC notes that 4096-bit RSA is recommended because a 15360-bit modulus would be needed for 256 bits of security, which is impractical.
sections.eli5: A stronger fingerprint is only useful if the lock it guards is strong too, so the RFC pairs each fingerprint size with a matching key size.
